newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech crown stable as govt ponders reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech crown stable as govt ponders reshuffle.

text.p: The Czech crown was stable on Wednesday with traders awaiting the outcome of talks aimed at forming a new cabinet and warning that further political instability could put further pressure on the currency.

The crown, which fell sharply on Tuesday after the central bank bowed to speculative pressure and allowed it to float, stood at 19.287 against the mark and 32.897 to the dollar at 1130 GMT, slightly stronger than in morning trade.

"The Czech crown is waiting for what will happen on the political side of things," said Milan Vavra of Komercni Banka. "Political detsabilisation is the most important thing for foreign investors so nobody is doing a lot of business in foreign exchange," he said.
Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus cancelled a visit to the Netherlands in order to press ahead with talks aimed at finalising a new government line-up.
Leaders of the three-party centre-right coalition were due to resume talks later on Wednesday, Klaus's office said.
Coalition leaders agreed last week to make changes to the cabinet after a sharp drop in its popularity sparked by an economic downturn and widespread reports of financial crime.
"If a new government will not be established in the near future, I expect that the crown will go lower again," said Vavra.

The crown fell about eight percent against the dollar and mark on Tuesday after the central bank, acting with U.S. and British markets closed for holidays, scrapped the band within which the crown fluctuated against a mark/dollar basket.
The crown had been under severe speculative selling pressure for 10 days, reflecting investor concern over burgeoning trade and current account deficits.
Emil Stava, head of derivatives marketing at Citibank in Prague, said that, apart from politics, investors were also waiting for high Czech interest rates to stabilise.
The CNB raised its key discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5 percent and left its Lombard rate at 50 percent on Monday.
"I expect a slowdown on the Czech market," he said adding that he expected the crown to settle at between 19.5 and 20 to the mark.
He said some foreign investors had suffered as a result of the central bank's move. "I can imagine that for a couple of days there will be little activity on the market."
Pavel Pinkava of Nomura International in London said the crown could face further weakness in coming weeks.

"The moment interest rates drop, there will be another go at it," he said. "People who have got monmey to make are going to wait until the dust settles. There are just too many uncertainties," he said.
The Czech crown crisis has hit other currencies, notably the Slovak crown, Greek drachma, Polish zloty and Hungarian forint.

The National Bank of Slovakia effectively intervened by fixing the crown at 33.316 to the dollar and at 19.542 to the mark on Wednesday, implying a deviation from its basket midpoint of -0.67 percent.
At the time of calculation, the crown was trading at -6.50 percent against the midpoint. The crown immediately strengthened some 250 basis points.
The Bank of Greece intervened for the second consecutive day, selling 200 million ecus and 25 million marks to support the drachma, dealers said.
Polish finance minister Marek Belka said the main wave of foreign investor withdrawal from zloty instruments, sparked by the Czech crown's fall, was over.
